content.key_idea: Grace's receiver waits for a still-missing packet only until a computed deadline t*, because waiting past that point yields lower utility than decoding immediately with the packets already in hand.
content.reading_order: left to right along the time axis, following each sawtooth reset at a packet arrival, then down the decay curve to the deadline t*, comparing the high- and low-utility callouts on either side.

summary: Figure tex7 explains the deadline that governs when Grace's receiver decodes a frame. Utility (Q minus beta times elapsed time) rises sharply at each packet arrival and then decays; the curve is annotated with callouts marking the arrivals of the (i-1)th and ith packets. After the ith packet arrives at t_i, the receiver computes a deadline t* from the expected gain Q(i+1)-Q(i) of waiting for one more packet. If the (i+1)th packet arrives before t*, utility stays high; if it arrives after t*, the receiver instead decodes immediately with only i packets, and utility is low, no better than deciding at t_i. A red reference line marks that break-even utility level. The figure argues the receiver should wait longer only when the potential quality gain from one more packet is larger, but never past the point where waiting no longer pays off.
summary_zh: 图解释Grace接收端的解码截止时间机制：效用随时间衰减，每次收包跳升；计算出的t*之前收到下一包则效用高，之后到达则立即用已有i个包解码，效用较低。
notes: content.groups corrected from the prior 'logic' to 'anatomy': the drawn structure is a continuous utility-vs-time sawtooth curve (base timeline) annotated with speech-bubble callouts, not a state machine or decision flowchart with nodes and labelled branches, so it does not meet the v3 definition of the logic group even though it explains a threshold decision.
